title: Ἐν σταθμῷ τοῦ συβώτου
about: Odysseus follows the path Athena showed him to the farm of the swineherd Eumaeus. The poet describes the high walled yard, the twelve pens with their fifty sows each, the fewer boars, and the four dogs. The dogs run at the stranger; Odysseus sits down and drops his staff, and Eumaeus drives them off with stones and scolds the old man for the shame they nearly brought on him. He leads his guest into the hut, spreads a bed of brushwood and goatskin, and the unrecognised Odysseus thanks him. Eumaeus answers that all strangers and beggars come from Zeus, mourns his lost master, and cooks two piglets. As they eat he tells the beggar that the suitors devour the fat swine without fear of the gods, that his master's wealth was beyond that of any man, and begins to count the herds on the mainland and on Ithaca.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ ἐκ λιμένος προσέβη τρηχεῖαν ἀταρπὸν
χῶρον ἀν’ ὑλήεντα δι’ ἄκριας, ᾗ οἱ Ἀθήνη
πέφραδε δῖον ὑφορβόν, ὅ οἱ βιότοιο μάλιστα
κήδετο οἰκήων, οὓς κτήσατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
But he from the harbour stepped forward on a rough path,
up through wooded country, over the hilltops, where for him Athena
had-pointed-out the heavenly swineherd, who for him of the livelihood most
cared, of the servants whom had-acquired heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: But he stepped off from the harbour onto a rough path, up through wooded country and over the hilltops, to where Athena had pointed out to him the heavenly swineherd, who of the household servants that heavenly Odysseus had acquired cared most for his livelihood.
sentences.n: The ὁ after αὐτάρ is the pronoun ‘he’: Odysseus, leaving the harbour. τρηχεῖαν is Ionic for Attic τραχεῖαν ‘rough’; ἀταρπός is a path; ἄκριας is the accusative plural of ἄκρις ‘hilltop’, and ἀν’ is ἀνά ‘up’. ᾗ is ‘where’ and οἱ ‘for him’; πέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist of φράζω ‘point out’. ὑφορβός ‘swineherd’ is built on ὑπό and φέρβω ‘feed’. δῖος, ‘heavenly’, is the epithet the poem gives Odysseus in line 4; here it is given to the swineherd too and kept the same way. οἰκήων is the genitive plural of οἰκεύς ‘household servant’, and κήδετο ‘cared for’ takes the genitive βιότοιο ‘livelihood’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ἐνὶ προδόμῳ εὗρ’ ἥμενον, ἔνθα οἱ αὐλὴ
ὑψηλὴ δέδμητο, περισκέπτῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ,
καλή τε μεγάλη τε, περίδρομος·
sentences.i: He found him sitting in the vestibule, where his high yard had been built, on a site open to view from every side, fine and large, with room to run all round it;
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, the swineherd, whom Odysseus finds at once; for the next several units the poet describes his yard and animals before the action goes on. πρόδομος (προ- ‘before’ + δόμος ‘house’) is the space in front of the house proper, here ‘vestibule’. οἱ is ‘his’, and δέδμητο is the pluperfect passive of δέμω ‘build’. Two words are uncertain in sense: περισκέπτῳ means ‘to be seen on every side’ (or ‘commanding a view all round’), and the exact sense of περίδρομος, literally ‘running round’, is not known; ‘with room to run all round it’ is the usual guess. ἐνί is the epic form of ἐν.

sentences.t:
ἥν ῥα συβώτης
αὐτὸς δείμαθ’ ὕεσσιν ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος,
νόσφιν δεσποίνης καὶ Λαέρταο γέροντος,
ῥυτοῖσιν λάεσσι καὶ ἐθρίγκωσεν ἀχέρδῳ·
sentences.l:
which, then, the swineherd
himself built for the swine, while his lord was away,
apart from his mistress and the old man Laertes,
with hauled stones, and he topped it with wild-pear;
sentences.i: which the swineherd had built himself for the swine, while his lord was away, without his mistress or old Laertes, of hauled stones, and he capped it with wild pear;
sentences.n: ἥν ‘which’ is the yard of the last unit. δείμαθ’ is the aorist middle of δέμω ‘build’, elided (δείματο), with θ because the next word begins with a rough breathing. ὕεσσιν is the dative plural of ὗς ‘swine’, with the ending -εσσι. ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος is a genitive absolute, ‘his lord being away’; ἄναξ ‘lord’ is Odysseus. νόσφιν ‘apart from’ takes the genitive: Eumaeus built it on his own, without his mistress (δέσποινα; Penelope is meant but not named) or old Laertes. ῥυτοῖσιν λάεσσι is ‘with hauled stones’: ῥυτός is ‘dragged’ (from ἐρύω) and λᾶας ‘stone’. ἐθρίγκωσεν is from θριγκόω ‘top with a coping’ (θριγκός); ἄχερδος is a thorny wild pear, so the wall’s top was a thorn hedge.

sentences.t:
σταυροὺς δ’ ἐκτὸς ἔλασσε διαμπερὲς ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
πυκνοὺς καὶ θαμέας, τὸ μέλαν δρυὸς ἀμφικεάσσας·
sentences.l:
and stakes outside he drove, all the way through, here and there,
thick and close-set, the dark of the oak having split-around;
sentences.i: and outside it he drove stakes in an unbroken line, this way and that, thick and close together, after splitting the dark wood of an oak all round;
sentences.n: σταυρούς are ‘stakes’. ἔλασσε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ with a doubled σ for the metre. διαμπερές is ‘right through, without a break’, and ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘here and there’, that is on this side and that. τὸ μέλαν δρυός, ‘the dark of the oak’, is most likely the dark heartwood; ἀμφικεάσσας is the aorist participle of ἀμφικεάζω ‘split round’ (again with σσ), but the exact sense of the phrase is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἔντοσθεν δ’ αὐλῆς συφεοὺς δυοκαίδεκα ποίει
πλησίον ἀλλήλων, εὐνὰς συσίν·
sentences.l:
And inside the yard twelve pens he made,
close to one another, beds for the swine;
sentences.i: Inside the yard he made twelve pens, close to one another, as beds for the swine;
sentences.n: ἔντοσθεν is ‘inside’. συφεούς is the accusative plural of συφεός ‘pen, sty’, and δυοκαίδεκα is ‘twelve’ (δύο καὶ δέκα). ποίει is the imperfect of ποιέω without its augment. εὐνὰς συσίν, ‘beds for the swine’, stands in apposition to the pens; συσίν is the dative plural of σῦς.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ ἑκάστῳ
πεντήκοντα σύες χαμαιευνάδες ἐρχατόωντο,
θήλειαι τοκάδες·
sentences.i: and in each fifty swine, sleeping on the ground, were penned, females, brood sows;
sentences.n: ἑκάστῳ is ‘each’. ἐρχατόωντο ‘were penned’ is related to ἔρχατο in line 73 and has the Homeric stretched ending (-όωντο for Attic -ῶντο). χαμαιευνάδες ‘sleeping on the ground’ is from χαμαί ‘on the ground’ and εὐνή ‘bed’. θήλειαι ‘female’ and τοκάδες ‘breeding’ (from τίκτω ‘bear young’) together say these are sows that bear young.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἄρσενες ἐκτὸς ἴαυον,
πολλὸν παυρότεροι·
sentences.l:
and the males outside slept,
much fewer;
sentences.i: while the boars slept outside, and far fewer of them;
sentences.n: τοί is the pronoun ‘they’, in contrast with the females of the last unit. ἄρσενες are ‘males’. ἴαυον is the imperfect of ἰαύω ‘sleep, lie’. πολλὸν is an adverb ‘by much’, and παυρότεροι the comparative of παῦρος ‘few’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς γὰρ μινύθεσκον ἔδοντες
ἀντίθεοι μνηστῆρες, ἐπεὶ προΐαλλε συβώτης
αἰεὶ ζατρεφέων σιάλων τὸν ἄριστον ἁπάντων·
sentences.i: for the godlike suitors kept reducing them by eating them, since the swineherd was always sending them the best of all the well-fed fat hogs;
sentences.n: τούς is the pronoun ‘them’, the boars. μινύθεσκον is an iterative imperfect (the -σκον ending), ‘kept on diminishing’, and ἔδοντες ‘eating’ (ἔδω) says how. ἀντίθεοι ‘godlike’ is the house rendering, kept even for the suitors. προΐαλλε is the imperfect of προϊάλλω ‘send forth’. ζατρεφής ‘well-fed’ has the intensive prefix ζα-; the house table gives ‘sleek’ for the literal line and ‘well-fed’ for the prose. σίαλος is a fattened hog.

sentences.t: οἱ δὲ τριηκόσιοί τε καὶ ἑξήκοντα πέλοντο.
sentences.l: and they, three hundred and sixty, were.
sentences.i: and there were three hundred and sixty of them.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ ‘and they’ are the boars. τριηκόσιοι τε καὶ ἑξήκοντα is ‘three hundred and sixty’. Twelve pens of fifty sows make six hundred sows against these 360 boars, which is why the males are ‘far fewer’. πέλοντο is the imperfect of πέλομαι ‘be’.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δὲ κύνες, θήρεσσιν ἐοικότες αἰὲν ἴαυον
τέσσαρες, οὓς ἔθρεψε συβώτης, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.l:
And beside them dogs, to wild beasts like, always slept,
four, which raised the swineherd, chief of men.
sentences.i: Beside them four dogs, like wild beasts, always slept, which the swineherd, a chief of men, had reared.
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά with its last vowel dropped, ‘beside’. θήρεσσιν is the dative plural of θήρ ‘wild beast’, after ἐοικότες, the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’. ἴαυον ‘slept’ picks up line 16. ἔθρεψε is the aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν ‘chief of men’ is a stock phrase of rank, kept as the house rendering even though it describes a swineherd.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἀμφὶ πόδεσσιν ἑοῖς ἀράρισκε πέδιλα,
τάμνων δέρμα βόειον ἐϋχροές·
sentences.l:
And he himself about his own feet was fitting sandals,
cutting an ox-hide of good colour;
sentences.i: He himself was fitting sandals to his feet, cutting them from an ox-hide of good colour;
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘he himself’ sets Eumaeus at work against the dogs and the pens. ἑοῖς is the possessive ἑός ‘his own’, not the relative. ἀράρισκε is the imperfect of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, and πέδιλα are ‘sandals’. τάμνων is ‘cutting’ (τέμνω). ἐϋχροές, ‘of good colour’ (εὖ + χρώς), agrees with δέρμα ‘hide’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι
ᾤχοντ’ ἄλλυδις ἄλλος ἅμ’ ἀγρομένοισι σύεσσιν,
οἱ τρεῖς·
sentences.i: while the others, the three of them, went off, each in a different direction, with swine they had gathered;
sentences.n: οἱ ἄλλοι ‘the others’ are the herdsmen besides Eumaeus, four in all; οἱ τρεῖς ‘the three’ says which of them go off with the swine, and the fourth is sent to the city in the next unit. ᾤχοντ’ is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, and ἄλλυδις ἄλλος ‘one this way, another that’. ἀγρομένοισι is the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, dative plural in -οισι.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ τέταρτον ἀποπροέηκε πόλινδε
σῦν ἀγέμεν μνηστῆρσιν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ἀνάγκῃ,
ὄφρ’ ἱερεύσαντες κρειῶν κορεσαίατο θυμόν.
sentences.l:
and the fourth he had sent off to the city
to drive a hog to the overweening suitors, under compulsion,
so that, having slaughtered it, they might sate their heart with meats.
sentences.i: and the fourth he had sent to the city, to bring a hog to the overweening suitors under compulsion, so that they could slaughter it and sate their hearts on meat.
sentences.n: ἀποπροέηκε is the aorist of ἀποπροΐημι ‘send away’; πόλινδε is πόλιν ‘city’ with -δε ‘to’. ἀγέμεν is the epic infinitive ‘to drive, bring’ (Attic ἄγειν). ἀνάγκῃ ‘under compulsion’ says the suitors force this supply from him. ὑπερφίαλοισιν ‘overweening’ is the house rendering. ὄφρα with the aorist optative κορεσαίατο (from κορέννυμι ‘sate’) gives purpose; κρειῶν is the uncontracted genitive plural of κρέας ‘flesh’. ἱερεύσαντες ‘having slaughtered’ keeps the meal in view, as the table fixes.

sentences.t: ἐξαπίνης δ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἴδον κύνες ὑλακόμωροι.
sentences.l: Suddenly, then, the barking dogs saw Odysseus.
sentences.i: Suddenly the barking dogs caught sight of Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἴδον is an unaugmented aorist, ‘saw’ (Attic εἶδον). Ὀδυσῆα is Odysseus; the poem writes the name now with one σ and now with two, as the metre needs. ὑλακόμωροι is a stock epithet whose second half is not understood: the first element is ὑλάω ‘bark’, but -μωρος has no known meaning, so the translation keeps only ‘barking’ and does not guess the rest. ἐξαπίνης is ‘suddenly’.

sentences.t: οἱ μὲν κεκλήγοντες ἐπέδραμον·
sentences.l: They, for their part, clamouring, ran at him;
sentences.i: They ran at him, clamouring;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν ‘they, for their part’ is answered by αὐτάρ ‘but’ in the next unit. κεκλήγοντες is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘cry out, clamour’, a perfect that has a present sense. ἐπέδραμον is the aorist of ἐπιτρέχω ‘run at’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἕζετο κερδοσύνῃ, σκῆπτρον δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
sat down, with cunning, and the staff fell from his hand.
sentences.i: but Odysseus sat down, cunningly, and his staff dropped from his hand.
sentences.n: ἕζετο ‘sat down’ is a past tense of ἕζομαι. κερδοσύνῃ, ‘with cunning’ (κέρδος), marks the sitting down, not the dropping of the staff, as a deliberate ruse. σκῆπτρον is his staff (the beggar’s staff of the previous part), οἱ is ‘from him’, and ἔκπεσε ‘fell out’ takes the genitive χειρός ‘from his hand’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα κεν ᾧ πὰρ σταθμῷ ἀεικέλιον πάθεν ἄλγος·
sentences.l: Then beside his own steading an unseemly pain he would have suffered;
sentences.i: Then, at his own steading, he would have suffered an unseemly pain;
sentences.n: ἔνθα here is ‘then, in that case’, not ‘there’. With κεν the aorist πάθεν (‘he would have suffered’, unaugmented) is the unfulfilled past. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’, and its owner is Odysseus: the steading is his own property, the place where he is nearly mauled. σταθμός is a standing-place, here a farmstead; πὰρ is παρά ‘beside’. ἀεικέλιον ‘unseemly’ is the house rendering.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ συβώτης ὦκα ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι μετασπὼν
ἔσσυτ’ ἀνὰ πρόθυρον, σκῦτος δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.l:
but the swineherd quickly, on swift feet, hastening after,
rushed up through the forecourt, and the leather fell from his hand.
sentences.i: But the swineherd hurried after them on swift feet, rushed up through the forecourt, and the leather dropped from his hand.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ brings the rescue. ὦκα is ‘quickly’; ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι is ‘on swift feet’, with the dative ending -οῖσι. μετασπών is a participle of a rare verb; ‘hastening after’ is its usual gloss. ἔσσυτ’ is the aorist of σεύομαι ‘rush’, and πρόθυρον is the forecourt before the door. σκῦτος ‘leather’ is the hide he was cutting in line 24. The clause repeats line 31 almost word for word, σκῦτος for σκῆπτρον: both men let something drop from the hand.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ὁμοκλήσας σεῦεν κύνας ἄλλυδις ἄλλον
πυκνῇσιν λιθάδεσσιν·
sentences.l:
Them, for his part, having shouted at, he chased off, the dogs, one this way, one that,
with thick stones;
sentences.i: He shouted at the dogs and drove them off in every direction with showers of stones;
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν ‘them’ is the dogs, named in apposition by κύνας. ὁμοκλήσας is ‘having shouted at (them)’ in a threatening cry. σεῦεν is the imperfect of σεύω ‘chase’. ἄλλυδις ἄλλον ‘one this way, one that’ echoes line 25. πυκνῇσιν λιθάδεσσιν shows two dative plural endings, -ῃσιν and -εσσιν; λιθάς is ‘stone’ and πυκνός ‘thick’, so volleys of stones.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ προσέειπεν ἄνακτα·
sentences.l: and he addressed the lord:
sentences.i: and he spoke to his lord:
sentences.n: ὁ δέ ‘and he’ is the swineherd. ἄνακτα is the accusative of ἄναξ ‘lord’. Eumaeus does not know who the old man is; the narrator, who does, calls him ‘lord’ (the swineherd’s master). The edition ends this line with a raised point and the speech begins in the next line; the Greek has no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον, ἦ ὀλίγου σε κύνες διεδηλήσαντο
ἐξαπίνης, καί κέν μοι ἐλεγχείην κατέχευας.
sentences.l:
“Old man, indeed within a little the dogs mauled you
suddenly, and you would have poured-down disgrace upon me.
sentences.i: “Old man, suddenly the dogs very nearly mauled you, and you would have poured disgrace upon me.
sentences.n: The swineherd speaks; the poet names him only at line 55. ὦ γέρον ‘Old man’ is how he addresses a stranger of years. ἦ ὀλίγου is ‘within a little’: the dogs very nearly did it. διεδηλήσαντο is the aorist middle of διαδηλέομαι ‘tear apart’. καί κεν with the aorist κατέχευας is ‘you would have poured down’ (unfulfilled past): disgrace is poured as water is, an image the house rendering keeps. μοι is ‘upon me’.

sentences.t: καὶ δέ μοι ἄλλα θεοὶ δόσαν ἄλγεά τε στοναχάς τε·
sentences.l: And moreover other things to me the gods have given, pains and groans;
sentences.i: And besides, the gods have given me other things: pains and groans;
sentences.n: καὶ δέ is ‘and moreover’. δόσαν is unaugmented ἔδοσαν, aorist of δίδωμι. ἄλγεά τε στοναχάς τε ‘both pains and groans’ says what the ἄλλα ‘other things’ are; στοναχή is ‘groaning’.

sentences.t:
ἀντιθέου γὰρ ἄνακτος ὀδυρόμενος καὶ ἀχεύων
ἧμαι, ἄλλοισιν δὲ σύας σιάλους ἀτιτάλλω
ἔδμεναι·
sentences.i: for I sit here mourning and grieving for my godlike lord, while for others I raise fat swine to eat;
sentences.n: Eumaeus speaks of his lost master to the man he does not know to be that master. ἀντιθέου ἄνακτος is the genitive after the participles: ‘for my godlike lord’ (ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ is the house word). ὀδυρόμενος καὶ ἀχεύων is ‘lamenting and grieving’. ἧμαι is ‘I sit’. ἄλλοισιν is ‘for others’, ἀτιτάλλω ‘I rear’, and ἔδμεναι is the epic infinitive (Attic ἐσθίειν) ‘for them to eat’. σίαλος ‘fat’ as in line 19.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ κεῖνος ἐελδόμενός που ἐδωδῆς
πλάζετ’ ἐπ’ ἀλλοθρόων ἀνδρῶν δῆμόν τε πόλιν τε,
εἴ που ἔτι ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.l:
but that man, longing, perhaps, for food,
wanders over the land and city of men of other speech,
if somewhere he still lives and sees the light of the sun.
sentences.i: but he, perhaps wanting food, is wandering in the land and city of men of another tongue, if somewhere he is still alive and sees the light of the sun.
sentences.n: κεῖνος is ‘that man’, Odysseus. ἐελδόμενος ‘longing for’ takes the genitive ἐδωδῆς ‘food’; που is ‘perhaps’. πλάζετ’ is πλάζεται, the passive of πλάζω ‘drive off course’, the verb of the proem. ἀλλόθροος ‘of other speech’ (ἄλλος ‘other’ + θρόος ‘speech’) is the house ‘men of another tongue’. ζώει is uncontracted (Attic ζῇ); ὁρᾷ ‘sees’; φάος ἠελίοιο is ‘the light of the sun’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἕπεο, κλισίηνδ’ ἴομεν, γέρον, ὄφρα καὶ αὐτός,
σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο κορεσσάμενος κατὰ θυμόν,
εἴπῃς ὁππόθεν ἐσσὶ καὶ ὁππόσα κήδε’ ἀνέτλης.
sentences.l:
But follow; to the hut let us go, old man, so that you too, yourself,
having sated yourself of food and of wine, in heart,
may tell whence you are and how many sorrows you have endured.”
sentences.i: But follow me, old man, and let us go to the hut, so that you too, once you have eaten and drunk as your heart desires, may tell me where you are from and how many sorrows you have borne.”
sentences.n: ἕπεο is the imperative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ (Attic ἕπου). κλισίηνδε is κλισίη ‘hut’ with -δε ‘to’. ἴομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘let us go’ (Attic ἴωμεν), and εἴπῃς the subjunctive after ὄφρα ‘so that’. σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο are genitives of what one is filled with after κορεσσάμενος ‘having sated oneself’; κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in heart, as the heart wishes’. ἐσσί is ‘you are’ (Attic εἶ), and κήδεα ‘sorrows’. The guest is to eat first and tell who he is afterwards.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν κλισίηνδ’ ἡγήσατο δῖος ὑφορβός,
εἷσεν δ’ εἰσαγαγών, ῥῶπας δ’ ὑπέχευε δασείας,
ἐστόρεσεν δ’ ἐπὶ δέρμα ἰονθάδος ἀγρίου αἰγός,
αὐτοῦ ἐνεύναιον, μέγα καὶ δασύ.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, to the hut he led the way, the heavenly swineherd,
and sat him down, having brought him in, and thick twigs he spread beneath,
and over it he spread the hide of a shaggy wild goat,
his own bedding, large and thick.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the heavenly swineherd led the way to the hut, brought him in and sat him down, spread thick twigs beneath him, and laid over it the hide of a shaggy wild goat, his own bedding, large and thick.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is the house rendering. εἷσεν is the aorist of ἵζω in its causal sense ‘made him sit’. ῥῶπας is ‘twigs’ (ῥώψ, the word the house table renders ‘twigs’ at 10.166), ὑπέχευε ‘spread beneath’ (ὑποχέω) and δασείας ‘thick’. ἐπὶ … ἐστόρεσεν is tmesis, ἐπιστορέννυμι ‘spread over’. ἰονθάς is a rare word taken to mean ‘shaggy’; its sense is only guessed. αὐτοῦ is ‘his own’ (genitive of αὐτός) and ἐνεύναιον ‘bedding’, what one lies on.

sentences.t:
χαῖρε δ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὅττι μιν ὣς ὑπέδεκτο, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l:
and was glad, Odysseus,
that him thus he had received, and spoke a word and called him by name:
sentences.i: And Odysseus was glad that he had received him so, and he spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: χαῖρε here is a past tense, ‘was glad’, not the greeting ‘welcome’. ὅττι is ὅτι ‘because’. ὑπέδεκτο is a short aorist of ὑποδέχομαι ‘receive as a host’ (line 54 has the second person ὑπέδεξο). The whole formula ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν, ‘spoke a word and called him by name’, is kept as the house rendering, although Odysseus in fact addresses his host only as ‘stranger’.

sentences.t:
Ζεύς τοι δοίη, ξεῖνε, καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι
ὅττι μάλιστ’ ἐθέλεις, ὅτι με πρόφρων ὑπέδεξο.
sentences.l:
“May Zeus give you, stranger, and the other immortal gods,
what most you wish, because me, ready-minded, you received.”
sentences.i: “May Zeus grant you, stranger, and the other immortal gods, what you most wish, because you have received me with a ready mind.”
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks. ξεῖνε ‘stranger’ is what he calls his host: ξεῖνος serves for guest, host and stranger alike, and each man here calls the other by it. τοι is ‘to you’ (σοι). δοίη is the aorist optative of δίδωμι, a wish. The line has two near-identical words: ὅττι (ὅ τι) ‘whatever’ and then ὅτι ‘because’. πρόφρων is ‘ready-minded’ (house). ὑπέδεξο is the second person of the short aorist of ὑποδέχομαι, the same aorist as ὑπέδεκτο at line 51.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The poet turns and speaks to Eumaeus as ‘you’: προσέφης is the second person where the formula usually has the third, προσέφη. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’. Εὔμαιε συβῶτα, ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’, is the first time the swineherd’s name appears in this part. συβώτης is ‘swineherd’, the same English as ὑφορβός.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, οὔ μοι θέμις ἔστ’, οὐδ’ εἰ κακίων σέθεν ἔλθοι,
ξεῖνον ἀτιμῆσαι·
sentences.l:
“Stranger, not for me is it right, not even if one worse than you came,
to dishonour a stranger;
sentences.i: “Stranger, it is not right for me, even if a worse man than you should come, to dishonour a stranger;
sentences.n: Eumaeus answers. θέμις is what is right by custom and the gods; ἔστ’ is ἔστι, and ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε with the vowel dropped. οὐδ’ εἰ … ἔλθοι is ‘not even if … should come’ (optative). κακίων σέθεν is ‘worse than you’: κακίων is the comparative of κακός, and σέθεν the genitive of comparison (Attic σοῦ). ἀτιμῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀτιμάω ‘dishonour’.

sentences.t:
πρὸς γὰρ Διός εἰσιν ἅπαντες
ξεῖνοί τε πτωχοί τε·
sentences.l:
for from Zeus are all
strangers and beggars;
sentences.i: for all strangers and beggars are from Zeus;
sentences.n: πρὸς Διός, ‘from Zeus’, means that the stranger comes from his side and under his care. εἰσιν ἅπαντες ‘all are’ has the two nominatives ξεῖνοι and πτωχοί ‘strangers and beggars’ as its subject.

sentences.t:
δόσις δ’ ὀλίγη τε φίλη τε
γίγνεται ἡμετέρη·
sentences.l:
and a gift is small and dear
that comes from us;
sentences.i: and a small gift from us is welcome;
sentences.n: δόσις is ‘gift’, and φίλη ‘dear, welcome’ agrees with it: a small gift is welcome because it is given in goodwill. ἡμετέρη is ‘our’, here ‘from us servants’; γίγνεται ‘comes to be’.

sentences.t:
ἡ γὰρ δμώων δίκη ἐστὶν
αἰεὶ δειδιότων, ὅτ’ ἐπικρατέωσιν ἄνακτες
οἱ νέοι.
sentences.i: for that is the way of servants, who are always afraid whenever the young lords hold sway.
sentences.n: ἡ is the article ‘the’; δίκη here is ‘custom, way’ (at line 84 it is ‘justice’). δμώων is the genitive plural of δμώς ‘servant, slave’, and δειδιότων the genitive plural of the perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’, agreeing with it. ὅτ’ ἐπικρατέωσιν is a subjunctive with the uncontracted ending -έωσιν (Attic -ῶσιν): ‘whenever they hold sway’. ἄνακτες ‘lords’ is the plural of the word used of Odysseus above; οἱ νέοι ‘the young ones’ stands in apposition.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ τοῦ γε θεοὶ κατὰ νόστον ἔδησαν,
ὅς κεν ἔμ’ ἐνδυκέως ἐφίλει καὶ κτῆσιν ὄπασσεν,
οἶκόν τε κλῆρόν τε πολυμνήστην τε γυναῖκα,
οἷά τε ᾧ οἰκῆϊ ἄναξ εὔθυμος ἔδωκεν,
sentences.l:
For truly of him, at least, the gods bound down the homecoming,
who would have loved me kindly and given me property,
a house and an allotment and a much-wooed wife,
such things as a good-hearted lord gives to his own servant,
sentences.i: Truly the gods have bound fast the homecoming of the man who would have loved me kindly and given me property, a house and an allotment and a much-wooed wife, such things as a good-hearted lord gives to his own servant,
sentences.n: Murray prints line 64 before line 63, and this edition follows him, so the line numbers here run 61, 62, 64, 63; the sense reads straight through in the order printed, since house, allotment and wife are what the lord gives, as οἷά τε says. ἦ γάρ ‘truly’; τοῦ γε ‘of that man’. κατὰ … ἔδησαν is taken as tmesis, καταδέω ‘bind down’, with νόστον as its object. ὅς κεν with a past tense is ‘who would have’; ἐνδυκέως ‘kindly’ is the house rendering, and ὄπασσεν is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘give’. κλῆρος is an allotment of land, πολυμνήστην ‘much-wooed’, εὔθυμος ‘good-hearted’, and οἰκῆϊ the dative of οἰκεύς, with the possessive ᾧ ‘his own’.

sentences.t:
ὅς οἱ πολλὰ κάμῃσι, θεὸς δ’ ἐπὶ ἔργον ἀέξῃ,
ὡς καὶ ἐμοὶ τόδε ἔργον ἀέξεται, ᾧ ἐπιμίμνω.
sentences.l:
who for him much may toil, and a god the work may make grow,
as also for me this work grows, at which I stay.
sentences.i: such a servant as toils hard for him, with a god to make the work grow, as this work of mine grows, the work I stay at.
sentences.n: ὅς takes up οἰκῆϊ: a servant ‘who’ works. κάμῃσι is the subjunctive of κάμνω ‘toil’, general, ‘whoever toils’. ἐπὶ … ἀέξῃ is tmesis: ἀέξω ‘make grow’ (Attic αὐξάνω). ὡς … ἀέξεται compares: Eumaeus’s own work grows in the same way. ᾧ ἐπιμίμνω is ‘at which I stay’ (ἐπιμίμνω is ἐπιμένω).

sentences.t: τῷ κέ με πόλλ’ ὤνησεν ἄναξ, εἰ αὐτόθ’ ἐγήρα·
sentences.l: Then much would have benefited me the lord, if here he had grown old;
sentences.i: My lord would have done me much good, if he had grown old here;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘so, on that account’. κε … ὤνησεν is ‘would have helped’, the aorist of ὀνίνημι ‘benefit’. αὐτόθ’ is ‘on the spot, here’, and ἐγήρα the aorist of γηράσκω ‘grow old’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὄλεθ’—ὡς ὤφελλ’ Ἑλένης ἀπὸ φῦλον ὀλέσθαι
πρόχνυ, ἐπεὶ πολλῶν ἀνδρῶν ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσε·
sentences.l:
But he perished—would that of Helen the race had perished away
utterly, since of many men the knees she loosed;
sentences.i: But he perished—would that the race of Helen had perished utterly, since she loosed the knees of many men;
sentences.n: ὄλεθ’ is ὄλετο, ‘he perished’ (unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, with the final vowel dropped and τ turned to θ before a rough breathing): Eumaeus speaks of his master’s death to the master himself. ὡς ὤφελλ’ … ὀλέσθαι is ‘would that … had perished’, ὤφελλε being from ὀφείλω, ‘ought’, used for a wish. ἀπὸ … ὀλέσθαι is tmesis, ἀπολέσθαι ‘perish away’; φῦλον is ‘race, tribe’, and πρόχνυ ‘utterly’, an adverb of obscure origin. ὑπὸ … ἔλυσε is tmesis for ‘loosed beneath’: to loose a man’s knees is to kill him. The subject of ἔλυσε is not stated; Helen is understood. The dash marks the break in the sentence.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ κεῖνος ἔβη Ἀγαμέμνονος εἵνεκα τιμῆς
Ἴλιον εἰς εὔπωλον, ἵνα Τρώεσσι μάχοιτο.
sentences.l:
For indeed that man went, for the sake of Agamemnon's honour,
to Ilios of the fine foals, that with the Trojans he might fight.”
sentences.i: For he too went, for the sake of Agamemnon's honour, to Ilios of the fine foals, to fight the Trojans.”
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’; κεῖνος ‘that man’. Ἀγαμέμνονος εἵνεκα τιμῆς is ‘for the sake of Agamemnon’s honour’, with εἵνεκα ‘for the sake of’ taking the genitive τιμῆς, and Ἀγαμέμνονος, which depends on τιμῆς, standing before it. Ἴλιον εἰς εὔπωλον, ‘to Ilios of the fine foals’, is the house rendering (εὖ ‘well’ + πῶλος ‘foal’); Ilios is Troy. ἵνα with the optative μάχοιτο gives purpose, and Τρώεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ζωστῆρι θοῶς συνέεργε χιτῶνα,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἐς συφεούς, ὅθι ἔθνεα ἔρχατο χοίρων.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, with a belt he swiftly bound up his tunic,
and set out to go to the pens, where the broods of piglets were shut up.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and quickly girded his tunic with a belt, and set out for the pens, where the broods of piglets were shut in.
sentences.n: ζωστήρ is a belt and χιτών the tunic; συνέεργε is the imperfect of συνείργω, here ‘was binding together’, that is girding up. θοῶς is ‘quickly’. βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is ‘he set out to go’ (ἴμεν is the infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’). ὅθι is ‘where’. ἔθνεα is ‘broods, droves’, and χοίρων the genitive plural of χοῖρος ‘piglet’. ἔρχατο is a pluperfect passive of εἴργω ‘shut in’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν ἑλὼν δύ’ ἔνεικε καὶ ἀμφοτέρους ἱέρευσεν,
εὗσέ τε μίστυλλέν τε καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειρεν.
sentences.l:
From there, taking two, he brought them and both he slaughtered,
singed them and cut them up and around spits he pierced them.
sentences.i: He took two from there, brought them in, slaughtered them both, singed them, cut them into pieces, and pierced them on spits.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’ (-θεν marks ‘from’); ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’, and δύ’ is δύο ‘two’. ἔνεικε is the aorist of φέρω ‘bring’ (Attic ἤνεγκε). ἱέρευσεν ‘slaughtered’ is the house rendering of ἱερεύω, which also means ‘sacrifice’; here the slaughter is for a meal. εὗσε ‘singed’ is from εὕω, ‘singe off the bristles’. μίστυλλε ‘cut up’ (μιστύλλω) and ἔπειρεν ‘pierced’ (πείρω) complete the work in order; ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν is ‘around spits’.

sentences.t:
ὀπτήσας δ’ ἄρα πάντα φέρων παρέθηκ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ
θέρμ’ αὐτοῖς ὀβελοῖσιν·
sentences.l:
And having roasted all of it, bringing it he set it before Odysseus
hot, with the very spits;
sentences.i: When it was all roasted he brought it and set it before Odysseus hot, spits and all;
sentences.n: ὀπτήσας is ‘having roasted’ (ὀπτάω), and παρέθηκ’ the aorist of παρατίθημι ‘set before’, with the dative Ὀδυσῆϊ. θέρμ’ is θερμά, neuter plural ‘hot’, agreeing with the meat. αὐτοῖς ὀβελοῖσιν is ‘with the very spits’ (αὐτός with the dative means ‘together with’): the meat arrives still on the spits.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἄλφιτα λευκὰ πάλυνεν·
sentences.l: and he sprinkled white barley-meal;
sentences.i: and sprinkled white barley-meal over it;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ here is Eumaeus again, not a change of subject. ἄλφιτα ‘barley-meal’ (white: ἄλφιτα λευκά, the house rendering) is what is sprinkled, πάλυνεν ‘sprinkled’ (παλύνω); what it is sprinkled on is not stated, and the meat is understood.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα κισσυβίῳ κίρνη μελιηδέα οἶνον,
αὐτὸς δ’ ἀντίον ἷζεν, ἐποτρύνων δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And in an ivy-wood bowl he mixed honey-sweet wine,
and himself opposite he sat, and, urging him on, addressed him:
sentences.i: He mixed honey-sweet wine in an ivy-wood bowl, and sat down opposite him, and, urging him on, spoke to him:
sentences.n: κίρνη is the imperfect of κίρνημι ‘mix’, without augment; wine was mixed with water before it was drunk, though the line does not say so. κισσύβιον ‘ivy-wood bowl’ follows the traditional explanation of the word, and μελιηδέα ‘honey-sweet’ is the accusative of μελιηδής. ἷζεν is ‘sat’ and ἀντίον ‘opposite’. ἐποτρύνων is ‘urging on’, προσηύδα ‘addressed’; the speech begins in the next line.

sentences.t:
ἔσθιε νῦν, ὦ ξεῖνε, τά τε δμώεσσι πάρεστι,
χοίρε’·
sentences.l:
“Eat now, stranger, what for servants is at hand,
piglet-meats;
sentences.i: “Eat now, stranger, what servants have at hand: piglet meat;
sentences.n: Eumaeus speaks again. ὦ ξεῖνε ‘stranger’; the interjection ὦ is not translated. τά τε is the relative ‘such things as’, with epic τε. πάρεστι is ‘is at hand’ (a singular verb with a neuter plural subject). δμώεσσι is the dative plural of δμώς ‘servant’. χοίρε’ is χοίρεα, the neuter plural built on χοῖρος ‘piglet’, so ‘piglet meat’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ σιάλους γε σύας μνηστῆρες ἔδουσιν,
οὐκ ὄπιδα φρονέοντες ἐνὶ φρεσὶν οὐδ’ ἐλεητύν.
sentences.l:
but the fat swine the suitors eat,
not minding in their minds retribution nor pity.
sentences.i: but the fat swine the suitors eat, taking no thought in their minds for retribution or for pity.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘but’. σιάλους σύας, ‘fat swine’, are what the suitors eat: μνηστῆρες ‘suitors’ is the subject of ἔδουσιν ‘eat’ (Attic ἐσθίουσιν). ὄπις is a rare word usually taken to mean ‘retribution’, the watching eye of the gods that punishes; its sense is not certain, and the word returns at line 88. ἐλεητύς is ‘pity’. φρονέοντες ‘minding, giving thought to’ and ἐνὶ φρεσίν ‘in their minds’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν σχέτλια ἔργα θεοὶ μάκαρες φιλέουσιν,
ἀλλὰ δίκην τίουσι καὶ αἴσιμα ἔργ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
Not indeed do cruel deeds the blessed gods love,
but justice they honour and the proper deeds of men.
sentences.i: The blessed gods do not love cruel deeds, but honour justice and the proper deeds of men.
sentences.n: σχέτλια ‘cruel’ is the house rendering. μάκαρες is ‘blessed’, and φιλέουσιν is the uncontracted form of φιλοῦσιν. δίκη here is ‘justice’ (compare ‘way, custom’ at line 59). τίουσι is ‘honour’ (τίω), and αἴσιμα ‘proper, in due measure’ comes from αἶσα ‘due share’.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὲν δυσμενέες καὶ ἀνάρσιοι, οἵ τ’ ἐπὶ γαίης
ἀλλοτρίης βῶσιν καί σφι Ζεὺς ληΐδα δώῃ,
πλησάμενοι δέ τε νῆας ἔβαν οἶκόνδε νέεσθαι,
καὶ μὲν τοῖς ὄπιδος κρατερὸν δέος ἐν φρεσὶ πίπτει.
sentences.l:
Indeed even ill-disposed and hostile men, who upon the land
of others go, and to them Zeus gives plunder,
and, having filled their ships, set out to go home,
on them too of retribution a strong fear in their minds falls.
sentences.i: Even men who are ill-disposed and hostile, who go onto a foreign land and to whom Zeus grants plunder, and who sail for home with their ships filled, even in them a strong fear of retribution falls.
sentences.n: καὶ μέν is ‘and indeed’. δυσμενέες ‘ill-disposed’ and ἀνάρσιοι ‘hostile’ (the house rendering) describe raiders. The relative clause is a general statement: βῶσιν (aorist subjunctive of βαίνω) and δώῃ (of δίδωμι) have no κεν, as usual in such Homeric generalizations, and ἔβαν is a gnomic aorist, ‘set out’ as a rule. ληΐς is ‘plunder’, accusative ληΐδα. πλησάμενοι is ‘having filled’, οἶκόνδε ‘homewards’ (-δε), and νέεσθαι the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι ‘go back’. ὄπις is ‘retribution’ again.

sentences.t:
οἵδε δὲ καί τι ἴσασι, θεοῦ δέ τιν’ ἔκλυον αὐδήν,
κείνου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, ὅτ’ οὐκ ἐθέλουσι δικαίως
μνᾶσθαι οὐδὲ νέεσθαι ἐπὶ σφέτερ’, ἀλλὰ ἕκηλοι
κτήματα δαρδάπτουσιν ὑπέρβιον, οὐδ’ ἔπι φειδώ.
sentences.l:
But these men know something too, and have heard some voice of a god,
that man's grievous destruction, since they are not willing justly
to woo nor to go back to their own, but at ease
devour his goods with exceeding violence, and there is no sparing.
sentences.i: But these men know something too: they have heard some voice of a god about his grievous destruction, since they refuse to woo justly or to go back to their own, but at their ease devour his goods with exceeding violence, and there is no sparing.
sentences.n: οἵδε ‘these here’, the suitors, are set against the raiders. ἴσασι is ‘know’ (perfect of οἶδα), and ἔκλυον ‘heard’. κείνου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, ‘that man’s grievous destruction’, stands in apposition to αὐδήν and says what the voice told; Eumaeus’s inference is that the suitors act like men who believe the master dead. ὅτ’ here is ‘since’. μνᾶσθαι is ‘to woo’ (μνάομαι); ἐπὶ σφέτερ’ is ‘to their own’, with the noun left out. ἕκηλοι is ‘at ease’; ὑπέρβιον ‘with exceeding violence’ is the house rendering of the adverb. οὐδ’ ἔπι is οὐδὲ ἔπεστι, ‘and there is not’; φειδώ is ‘sparing’.

sentences.t:
ὅσσαι γὰρ νύκτες τε καὶ ἡμέραι ἐκ Διός εἰσιν,
οὔ ποθ’ ἓν ἱρεύουσ’ ἱερήϊον, οὐδὲ δύ’ οἴω·
sentences.l:
For as many nights and days as are from Zeus,
never one do they slaughter, a victim, nor two, I think;
sentences.i: For through all the nights and days that Zeus sends, they never slaughter one victim, nor even two, I think;
sentences.n: ὅσσαι is ‘as many as’. ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’ reminds that days and nights are given by him, so the phrase means every single one. ἱρεύουσ’ is ἱρεύουσι, a short form of ἱερεύουσι ‘slaughter’; ἱερήϊον is ‘victim, animal for slaughter’. οὐδὲ δύ’ οἴω, ‘nor two, I think’ (οἴω is οἴομαι), implies that they kill more than two.

sentences.t: οἶνον δὲ φθινύθουσιν ὑπέρβιον ἐξαφύοντες.
sentences.l: and wine they use up with exceeding violence, drawing it off.
sentences.i: and they waste the wine with exceeding violence, drawing it off.
sentences.n: φθινύθουσιν is ‘waste, use up’. ἐξαφύοντες is ‘drawing off’ (ἐξαφύσσω, to draw wine out of a vessel). ὑπέρβιον is the same adverb as in line 92, and the same English.

sentences.t: ἦ γάρ οἱ ζωή γ’ ἦν ἄσπετος·
sentences.l: For truly his livelihood was boundless;
sentences.i: For his livelihood was boundless;
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. ζωή here is ‘livelihood, the means of living’, the same thing as βιότοιο in line 3, not ‘life’. γ’ is γε ‘indeed’. ἄσπετος ‘boundless’ is the house rendering.

sentences.t:
οὔ τινι τόσση
ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων, οὔτ’ ἠπείροιο μελαίνης
οὔτ’ αὐτῆς Ἰθάκης·
sentences.i: no hero, whether of the dark mainland or of Ithaca itself, had so much;
sentences.n: οὔ τινι is ‘to no one’ (dative), with τόσση ‘so great’ agreeing with ζωή. ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων is ‘of heroic men’, a partitive genitive. ἠπείροιο is the genitive in -οιο of ἤπειρος ‘mainland’, the land across the water from the island; μελαίνης ‘dark’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ ξυνεείκοσι φωτῶν
ἔστ’ ἄφενος τοσσοῦτον·
sentences.l:
nor of twenty men together
is there so much wealth;
sentences.i: not even twenty men together have so much wealth;
sentences.n: ξυνεείκοσι is ‘twenty together’ (σύν in its older form ξυν- + εἴκοσι). φωτῶν is the genitive plural of φώς ‘man’. ἄφενος is ‘wealth’, ἔστ’ is ἔστι ‘there is’, and τοσσοῦτον ‘so much’.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι καταλέξω.
sentences.l: and I will recount it to you.
sentences.i: and I will tell you all of it.
sentences.n: καταλέξω is the aorist subjunctive of καταλέγω ‘recount’; with κε it is a firm ‘I will’. τοι is ‘to you’.

sentences.t: δώδεκ’ ἐν ἠπείρῳ ἀγέλαι·
sentences.l: Twelve, on the mainland, herds;
sentences.i: On the mainland there are twelve herds;
sentences.n: δώδεκ’ is δώδεκα ‘twelve’, elided. ἠπείρῳ is ‘on the mainland’, and ἀγέλαι ‘herds’ (usually of cattle). The count begins here, and the next unit repeats the number three times, for flocks of sheep, droves of swine and herds of goats.

sentences.t:
τόσα πώεα οἰῶν,
τόσσα συῶν συβόσια, τόσ’ αἰπόλια πλατέ’ αἰγῶν
βόσκουσι ξεῖνοί τε καὶ αὐτοῦ βώτορες ἄνδρες.
sentences.l:
as many flocks of sheep,
as many droves of swine, as many wide herds of goats
tend strangers and his own herdsmen.
sentences.i: strangers and his own herdsmen tend as many flocks of sheep, as many droves of swine, as many wide herds of goats.
sentences.n: τόσα, τόσσα, τόσ’ are ‘as many’ (that is, twelve), repeated three times as a list. πώεα are ‘flocks of sheep’, συβόσια ‘droves of swine’ (compare συβώτης), and αἰπόλια ‘herds of goats’; πλατέ’ is πλατέα ‘wide, broad’, a herd of wide extent, that is a large one. βόσκουσι is ‘feed, tend’. ξεῖνοι are men from elsewhere, set against αὐτοῦ βώτορες ἄνδρες ‘his own herdsmen’ (αὐτοῦ is taken as the genitive of αὐτός, ‘his own’).

sentences.t:
ἐνθάδε δ’ αἰπόλια πλατέ’ αἰγῶν ἕνδεκα πάντα
ἐσχατιῇ βόσκοντ’, ἐπὶ δ’ ἀνέρες ἐσθλοὶ ὄρονται.
sentences.l:
And here wide herds of goats, eleven in all,
at the edge graze, and over them good men keep watch.
sentences.i: And here, at the edge, eleven wide herds of goats in all graze, and good men keep watch over them.
sentences.n: ἐνθάδε ‘here’, on the island, against ἐν ἠπείρῳ above. ἕνδεκα is ‘eleven’. ἐσχατιῇ ‘at the edge’ is the outlying land, the house ‘at the edge’. βόσκοντ’ is the elided middle ‘graze’. ἐπὶ … ὄρονται is tmesis, ‘keep watch over’ (the verb is related to ἐπίουρος ‘overseer’); ἐσθλοί ‘good’.

sentences.t:
τῶν αἰεί σφιν ἕκαστος ἐπ’ ἤματι μῆλον ἀγινεῖ,
ζατρεφέων αἰγῶν ὅς τις φαίνηται ἄριστος.
sentences.l:
Of these always for them each one for the day a beast brings,
of the sleek goats whichever appears best.
sentences.i: Each of these men brings them a beast every day, whichever of the well-fed goats looks best.
sentences.n: τῶν is ‘of these’, the herdsmen, and σφιν ‘to them’, the suitors (σφι again at line 108). ἐπ’ ἤματι is ‘for each day’ (ἦμαρ ‘day’). μῆλον is a head of small stock, sheep or goat; here it is a goat, as the genitive αἰγῶν shows. ἀγινεῖ is ‘brings’. ζατρεφέων is the genitive plural of ζατρεφής, ‘sleek’ in the literal line and ‘well-fed’ in the prose, as the house table has it. ὅς τις φαίνηται is a general relative with the subjunctive and no κεν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σῦς τάσδε φυλάσσω τε ῥύομαί τε,
καί σφι συῶν τὸν ἄριστον ἐῢ κρίνας ἀποπέμπω.
sentences.l:
But I these swine both guard and protect,
and to them of the swine the best, having judged well, I send off.
sentences.i: But I guard and protect these swine, and when I have judged well which is the best of them, I send it off to them.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ sets the swineherd’s own task beside the goatherds’. σῦς τάσδε is ‘these swine here’ (accusative plural of σῦς). φυλάσσω τε ῥύομαί τε is ‘both guard and protect’, two verbs for one care. τὸν ἄριστον is ‘the best’ and ἐῢ κρίνας ‘having judged well’; σφι ‘to them’, the suitors; ἀποπέμπω ‘send off’.
